map.Lessons 3-3, 3-4 & 3-5 — ratio tables, r: Lessons 3-3, 3-4 & 3-5 — ratio tables, ratio graphs, and comparing ratios. Four gates stand in the way of race day.
map.Previously: the team paint mixed true, a: Last time: the team paint was mixed right. The reader's unit rates made Juno our anchor. New glitch found: the supply tent.
map.Previously, in Episode 1: the crew earne: Last time, in Episode 1: the crew won a spot in the Courier Cup. Now it is training week. Race heats run all weekend. Someone has to feed the riders.
map.Race office gave us the snack stations f: We run the snack stops all week. The recipe card says 4 snack packs for every 10 riders.
map.Heat one is ten riders. Heat four is FIF: Heat one is ten riders. Heat four is FIFTY. I build tables, not magic.
map.Then build a different table — a ratio t: Then build a new kind of table: a ratio table. Make the recipe bigger. Never break it.
map.Equivalent ratios show the same relation: Equivalent ratios show the same match-up. To scale one: multiply BOTH amounts by the same number.
map.Sienna's notebook, snack-station page. O: Sienna's book. The snack page. One ratio, many sizes.
map.Heat two doubled the riders, so the pack: Heat two had twice the riders. So the packs doubled too. Ten to twenty is × 2. Four to eight is × 2. Same move, both rows.
map.Scaling protocol: find the multiplier on: How to scale: find the multiplier on the riders row. Then use the SAME multiplier on the packs row. If you add, the food runs out.
map.Reader — heat three and heat four are ro: Reader, heats three and four are here. Fill the last two columns!
map.The recipe card says 4 snack packs for e: The recipe card says 4 snack packs for every 10 riders. Heat three has 30 riders. Heat four has 50. Fill in the ratio table.
map.Conceptual: every column must be the SAM: Conceptual: each column must be the SAME ratio, scaled up. Multiply riders AND packs by the same factor. Adding the same amount to a column breaks it.
map.Aid station two, water duty: 2 cups for: Aid stop two, water job: 2 cups for every 1 rider. I drew the pour plan as a picture.
map.It's a ratio graph. Riders across, cups: It is a ratio graph. Riders go across. Cups go up. Test any point: (2, 4)? 2 × 2 = 4. On the line. (4, 7)? 2 × 4 = 8, not 7. Off the line.
map.Equivalent ratios plot as points on one: Equivalent ratios make points on one straight line. It goes through (0, 0): zero riders, zero cups. Here the rule is cups = 2 × riders.
map.Someone stuck five pins in my chart, rea: Someone put five pins in my chart, reader. Only TWO go on our line. Tap just those two.
map.Aid station two pours 2 cups for every 1: Aid stop two pours 2 cups for every 1 rider. So true points are on the line through (0, 0). There, cups = 2 × riders. Five pins are on the chart. Tap the TWO pins that fit the pour. Tap again to un-pick.
map.Conceptual: every point that fits the po: Conceptual: points that fit the pour make one straight line. It goes through (0, 0). Look at a pin's riders number. Its cups number must be just 2 × that.
map.Procedural: test each pin by doubling it: Procedural: test each pin. Double its riders. (2, 5): 2 × 2 = 4, but the pin says 5. Off the line. Keep testing until just two pass.
map.Juno has 3 podiums in 5 heats. Four beat: Juno has 3 podiums in 5 heats. Four beats three… right? …Right?
map.Counts lie when the heats don't match. D: Counts can trick you. The heats do not match. Divide. Make each record podiums per ONE heat. Then compare.
map.Rohan wins 6 of 8 game rounds: 6 ÷ 8 = 0: Rohan wins 6 of 8 game rounds: 6 ÷ 8 = 0.75 per round. Records turn into decimals. Decimals can be compared.
map.To compare ratio relationships with diff: Two ratios can have different totals. To compare them, find each rate per one. Then compare the decimals.
map.Divide both records, reader. Then make t: Divide both records, reader. Then make the call. Whose record is better?
map.The brag board: Team Torque has 4 podium: The brag board: Team Torque has 4 podium finishes in 8 heats. Juno has 3 in 5. Make each record podiums per heat (a decimal). Then make the call.
map.Conceptual: you can't compare podium COU: Conceptual: you can't compare podium COUNTS here. The teams rode a different number of heats. First make each record podiums per ONE heat. Then the decimals can go head to head.
Procedural: Torque: 4 ÷ 8. Juno: 3 ÷ 5. Write each as a decimal. Then compare them.
map.Friday evening. The race office pins a n: Friday night. The race office pins up a notice. A rival station pins up a brag.
map.Triple the riders means triple EVERY col: Three times the riders? Then triple EACH column. Same recipe. Bigger stage. I can build that.
map.And Station Six just talked trash about: And Station Six just put down our pour. Scale the table. Read the line. Judge the rates. Boss fight!
map.Tomorrow the field triples and Juno ride: Tonight, we lock the supply plan. Then the field triples. Juno rides for a spot in the finals.
map.Three locks: scale the table, read the l: Three locks: scale the table, read the line, judge the pour. Reader leads.
map.Boss Gate: triple the 50-rider column, r: Boss Gate: triple the 50-rider column. Read the cups line at 12 riders. Then check Station Six's "most generous" claim. Use a rate.
map.BOSS GATE. Three locks. Qualifier day do: BOSS GATE. Three locks. Race day will not wait for small tables.
map.Qualifier day triples every heat, and St: Race day triples every heat. Station Six still brags. Three locks stand before the start horn:
map.Read the cups line when 12 riders roll i: Read the cups line at 12 riders: cups =
map.Station Six mixes 5 cups per 2 riders; w: Station Six mixes 5 cups per 2 riders. We pour 2 cups per 1 rider. Whose riders get more cups per rider?
map.Conceptual: tripling a heat triples BOTH: Conceptual: triple a heat? Then triple BOTH rows of its column. Riders and packs go up together. And the cups line never bends. Cups stay 2 × riders, even off the chart. For pours, compare cups per ONE rider.
map.Procedural: Lock 1: the 50-rider column: Procedural: Lock 1: the 50-rider column had 20 packs. Find 20 × 3. Lock 2: 2 × 12. Lock 3: 5 ÷ 2. Then compare it to our 2.
map.Sixty packs out, every cup poured on the: Sixty packs out. Each cup poured on the line. And Juno just made the final!
Brag board news: 0.6 per heat beats 0.5. Torque filed a complaint against… division.
map.Don't celebrate yet. The finals course m: Do not cheer yet. The map for the finals just came. It is in MILES.
map.Ratio tables.Every column is the same ra: Ratio tables.Each column is the same ratio, scaled. Find the multiplier on one row. Use it on the other. 4 : 10 stays 4 : 10 for ten riders or fifty.
map.Ratio graphs.Equivalent ratios plot as a: Ratio graphs.Equivalent ratios make a straight line through (0, 0). A point fits cups = 2 × riders. Or it is off the line. No in-between.
map.Comparing ratios.Different totals? Divid: Comparing ratios.Different totals? Divide each to get a rate per one. Then compare the decimals. 3 in 5 beats 4 in 8.
map.Adding is not scaling.Adding the same am: Adding is not scaling.Add the same amount to both rows? The recipe breaks. Multiply both rows? It stays true.
map.\"A recipe doesn't change when the crowd: "A recipe does not change when the crowd does. Only the multiplier does." — A.V.
map.completed Unit 3 · Episode 2: The Scalin: beat Unit 3 · Episode 2: The Scaling Stage. They can use ratio tables and graphs. They can compare ratios.
map.Episode 3 — Across the Line — waits at t: Up next is Episode 3: Across the Line. It is at the finish.
map.A different table: the info booth hands: A new table. The info desk gives out 3 maps for each 12 people.
map.For 60 visitors: 12 × 5 = 60, so maps =: For 60 people: 12 × 5 = 60, so maps = 3 × 5 = 15. Same multiplier, both rows. Each column simplifies back to 3 : 12.
map.Your turn — same idea, different numbers: Your turn. Same idea, new numbers:
map.Using 3 maps : 12 visitors, how many map: Use 3 maps : 12 people. How many maps for 48 people?
map.A different station pours 3 cups per rid: A new station pours 3 cups per rider. Its line is cups = 3 × riders.
map.Test (5, 14): 3 × 5 = 15, not 14 ✗ — tha: Test (5, 14): 3 × 5 = 15, not 14 ✗. That pin is off the line. Two fit, one fails.
map.At 3 cups per rider, how many cups shoul: It is 3 cups per rider. The pin is at 6 riders. How many cups?
map.Two snack stands: Stand A sold out 2 of: Two snack stands. Stand A sold out 2 of its 5 trays. Stand B sold out 3 of its 4.
map.0.75 > 0.4 — B is the stronger seller ev: 0.75 > 0.4. B sells better, with fewer trays. Use rates, not raw counts.
map.A team podiums 5 times in 8 heats. What: A team gets 5 podiums in 8 heats. What is its rate per heat as a decimal?
map.A different station: 5 packs : 20 riders: A new station: 5 packs : 20 riders, with a 3-cups-per-rider line.
map.Triple the column: 20 × 3 = 60 riders an: Triple the column: 20 × 3 = 60 riders and 5 × 3 = 15 packs. Read the line at 7 riders: 3 × 7 = 21 cups.
map.A rival pours 7 cups per 2 riders: 7 ÷ 2: A rival pours 7 cups per 2 riders: 7 ÷ 2 = 3.5 per rider. 3.5 > 3. So the rival gives more per rider.
map.A 5 packs : 20 riders column is scaled ×: A 5 packs : 20 riders column is scaled × 4. How many packs for 80 riders?
map.12 packs for 30 riders, 20 for 50 — ever: 12 packs for 30 riders, 20 for 50. Each column is still 4 : 10. Heat four eats!
map.16 comes from ADDING 4 each column — but: 16 comes from ADDING 4 each column. But the riders went from 30 to 50, not 30 to 40. Find the multiplier from the first column: 10 → 50 is × what?
map.At least one cell breaks the 4 : 10 reci: At least one cell breaks the 4 : 10 recipe. Find each column's multiplier on the riders row. Then use it on the packs row.
map.(3, 6) and (5, 10) — both sit exactly on: (3, 6) and (5, 10) both sit right on cups = 2 × riders. The pour line holds. Stock up!
map.0.6 podiums per heat beats 0.5. Three-in: 0.6 podiums per heat beats 0.5. Three in five beats four in eight. Sorry, brag board.
map.Divide podiums by heats for each record: Divide podiums by heats for each record. Each answer is per ONE heat. It is a decimal less than 1.
map.Your rates are right… now compare the de: Your rates are right… now compare the decimals. Which number is bigger? Whose is it?
map.Lock 1 holds. The column scales by × 3 o: Lock 1 is shut. The column scales by × 3 on BOTH rows. 50 riders became 150. So 20 packs become…
map.Lock 2 holds. The line never bends: cups: Lock 2 is shut. The line never bends: cups = 2 × riders, even at 12.
map.Lock 3 holds. Per rider: 5 cups ÷ 2 ride: Lock 3 is shut. Per rider: 5 cups ÷ 2 riders = ? Compare that decimal to our 2 cups per rider.
map.ALL LOCKS OPEN. 60 packs, 24 cups — and: ALL LOCKS OPEN. 60 packs, 24 cups. And yes, 5 ÷ 2 = 2.5 beats our 2. So Station Six pours more per rider. Honest math both ways. Race day is FED!
